lines: I remember opening my eyes and smelling clean straw. You were beside me.
You fed me broth until my hands stopped shaking.
The first morning after the cure felt like spring after a hard frost.
You brought me water before I knew how thirsty I was.
I heard the animals outside and understood that I was home.
You kept the room warm through the night.
I remember your muddy boots by the bed more clearly than the fever.
The cure gave me my life back. Your patience helped me live in it again.
You waited until I could stand, then walked me to the door.
My hands knew how to hold seed before my mind knew the season.
You never made me feel ashamed of how weak I was.
The first bread I tasted afterward came from your hand.
I woke afraid of hunger, and you showed me a full bowl.
You told me the fields could wait. I needed to hear that.
I remember sunlight on the floor and your shadow crossing it with water.
You stayed until I recognized the village sounds again.
Every healthy crop I see reminds me that recovery can begin small.
I could not have tended myself through that sickness. Thank you.
You gave me quiet when I needed it and company when I asked.
I am back in the fields because you carried me through the worst night.
I remember wet cloth on my forehead. Were you the one changing it?
Your face belongs to that day, but I cannot place where.
There was a bowl beside the bed and dirt under somebody's nails.
Did you open the shutters, or did I only dream of morning?
I remember hearing a hoe strike soil outside while someone held the cup.
The cure is a bitter taste surrounded by missing hours.
People say you found me. I wish I remembered being found.
I knew the smell of wheat before I knew my own name again.
Were you there when I tried to stand too soon?
I keep seeing a lantern and your coat beside it.
Someone told me the crops had been watered. Was that you?
My hands remember gripping yours even when my mind does not.
I woke certain I had missed an entire season.
The room was warm, but I could not stop shivering.
Your voice was in the room. The words are gone.
I remember asking for bread and then falling asleep again.
The day returns in pieces whenever I pass that doorway.
I know you helped because everyone says so, and because your face feels safe.
Please tell me what happened slowly. The memories tangle easily.
I cannot name every moment, but I know I survived it with help.
I know you saved me. I still need you to stay near the doorway.
Please do not reach for me without asking.
The cure worked, but the fear did not leave at once.
I remember being held down so I would not hurt myself.
Your face is tied to a night I cannot bear to revisit yet.
I am thankful. I am also frightened. Both can be true.
Let me keep the table between us while we speak.
The smell of that medicine still makes my chest tighten.
I need to see the way outside.
Do not bring the bottle near me again.
I believe you came to help, but my hands still shake around you.
Some mornings I wake certain the sickness has returned.
Please keep your voice low. Loud words make the room feel smaller.
I cannot talk about what I did while I was ill.
Give me a little time before asking for trust.
I want to remember the farm, not the bed where I woke.
Stand there. I can listen better when I have room.
You did the right thing. My fear has not caught up with that truth.
If I end this conversation suddenly, do not follow me.
Thank you for the cure. Please let me recover at my own pace.
